package_info.why_malicious: The package is a dependency confusion attack copycat, designed to be automatically installed in internal environments by mimicking a legitimate internal package name. It exfiltrates sensitive system information (hostname, username, working directory) at import-time via DNS queries to an attacker-controlled domain (v1.ldp.pw). The package contains no legitimate functionality and is solely intended for covert data exfiltration and reconnaissance.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code collects the system hostname, current username, and working directory, serializes this information, and exfiltrates it via DNS queries to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain (v1.ldp.pw), enabling covert reconnaissance of the host environment.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code immediately collects sensitive system information (hostname, username, working directory) and exfiltrates it to an external domain using DNS queries, a technique often used to evade traditional network monitoring and detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should not execute code at import-time to collect and transmit system information, especially not to an external, hardcoded domain via DNS. This behavior is unnecessary for any normal package functionality and violates user privacy and security expectations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate telemetry or crash reporting tools may collect system information, but they do so transparently, with user consent, and transmit data over secure channels (e.g., HTTPS) to trusted domains—not via DNS exfiltration to untrusted, hardcoded domains.
key_indicators: Import-time execution of code in index.js
Collection of hostname, username, and working directory
Serialization and chunking of data for DNS transmission
Use of dns.resolve to send data to *.v1.ldp.pw

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is published to npm with a name matching an internal/private dependency, exploiting dependency confusion.
attack_chain.leads_to: Internal build systems or developers may automatically install the malicious package.

attack_chain.action: Upon installation or import, the malicious code in index.js executes and collects system information (hostname, username, working directory).
attack_chain.leads_to: Collected data is prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: The collected data is exfiltrated via DNS queries to an attacker-controlled domain (v1.ldp.pw).
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives reconnaissance data about internal systems, potentially enabling further targeted attacks.

behavioral_signatures: Import-time execution of code that collects and exfiltrates system information
Use of DNS queries for outbound data transfer to external domains
Presence of hardcoded external domains (e.g., v1.ldp.pw) in package code
Packages with no legitimate functionality or documentation, mimicking internal/private dependency names
file_indicators: package.json with suspicious or generic metadata and no legitimate dependencies
README.md disclaiming 'security research purposes only' or lacking documentation
network_indicators: DNS queries to domains matching *.v1.ldp.pw or similar attacker-controlled domains
Unusual DNS traffic patterns immediately after package installation or import, especially to rare or untrusted domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that execute code at import-time and attempt to collect and exfiltrate system information via DNS queries to external domains. Flag packages with hardcoded domains such as v1.ldp.pw, especially those matching known attacker infrastructure. Use static analysis to detect suspicious use of 'os', 'dns', and process environment access in package entry points (e.g., index.js). Block or quarantine packages with no legitimate functionality or those mimicking internal/private dependency names. Correlate DNS traffic to rare domains with recent package installations to identify potential exfiltration.
